Can blue-enriched office lighting improve focus?

A controlled crossover experiment found less subjective sleepiness under blue-enriched light, but no extra concentration benefit.

More stimulating light does not necessarily mean better thinking. An experiment in two windowless office rooms tested what actually changes.

The experiment

Gagné and colleagues studied 30 healthy adults (19 women; mean age 23.4) in a counterbalanced crossover experiment. Each person spent 50 minutes under conventional 3,500 K fluorescent light (159 melanopic EDI lux) and blue-enriched 5,000 K LED light (263 melanopic EDI lux), on different days at similar times. Vertical photopic illuminance was comparable: 335 versus 344 lux. Researchers measured subjective sleepiness (KSS), concentration (d2-R), contrast sensitivity, and lighting preference.

The numbers

Subjective sleepiness decreased significantly over time only in the blue-enriched condition (p = 0.03; Cohen's d = 0.42); this within-condition finding is not proof of a significant between-condition advantage. Concentration improved under both lights (p < 0.0001), without a significant difference between lighting conditions (p = 0.79). Contrast sensitivity was worse under blue-enriched light (p = 0.01; d = 0.50). Participants preferred conventional light (p = 0.004; d = 0.56).

Architecture and doctoral research

Light spectra should be designed for both alertness and visual comfort, not reduced to a single 'optimal' Kelvin value. A useful next study would manipulate melanopic exposure independently of room appearance and lamp type, and test cognitive outcomes over weeks.

What the study cannot show

The small, young sample, 50-minute exposure, two different rooms and lamp technologies, repeated tests, and multiple comparisons limit generalization. No EEG, MRI, synapse, gene-expression or epigenetic changes were measured. The experiment tests short-term perception and performance, not neuroplasticity.
